2. The petitioner-decree holder as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 60 of 1989 in the Court of the Assistant Judge Sherpur, Bogra impleading the opposite parties as defendants praying for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession after demolition of the homestead standing on the suit land measuring 1.76 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.24113 corresponding to M.R.R. Khatian Nos. 202, 204, 215 and plot No. 75 of Mouza Sherun. The said suit was decreed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 6.2.93. 

 7. It appears that Title Suit No. 60 of 1989 was a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession Son demolition of structure on the portion of the suit land. The suit was decreed on contest against several defendants and ex parte also against several defendants. The present opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 were the defendant 74, 76 and 77 of the earlier suit and order No. 28 dated 2.5.90 of Title Suit No. 60 of 1989 shows that the summons of the said suit was duly served on the said defendants, who are opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 in the present application and plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 90 of 1999. It thus prima facie appears that the summons of the earlier suit Was duly served on the defendant No. 74, 76 and 77 who filed Other Suit No. 90 of 1999 after the contesting defendants lost the battle of the earlier suit up to the High Court Division, The opposite party No. 1 to 3 as plaintiffs of Other Suit No. 90 of 1999 asserted that the decree was obtained without service of summons on them. This question is to be decided at the time of trial of the suit on taking evidence. But appears prima facie that the summons of the earlier suit was duly served on the defendant No. 74, 76 and 77 who had chosen not to contest the suit and after the discharge of the Rule by the High Court Division, the said defendants as plaintiffs filed the present suit on the ground of non-service of summons. In the facts of the case mere filing of the suit challenging the decree by the non-contesting defendants should not be a ground for stay of all further proceeding of the execution case. The contested decree should not be frustrated only due to institution of a suit by the non-contesting defendants. The plaintiffs who got the decree, which was maintained up to the High Court Division, should be allowed to enjoy the fruit of the decree and if the decree is subsequently set aside, the successful party has his remedy under the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 10. On a perusal of all the provisions of Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984 it appears that it was not the intention of the law-makers to prohibit eviction of any one of any homestead situated in a rural area in execution of a decree of the competent civil Court for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. "Any land used as a homestead by its owner ...." as provided in section 6 of the Land Reforms Ordinance does not remain owner of the homestead when a declaration of title is passed against such person by a competent civil court. Section 6 of Land Worms Ordinance 1984 does not therefore prohibit the eviction of persons found to be evictable by the competent civil Court in a legally constituted suit. In the present case the suit was filed for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the competent civil Court found that the plaintiff is the owner of the suit properties including the homestead standing in a portion of the suit land and further found that the plaintiff is entitled to recovery of possession of the suit land of the said suit. This decree of the trial Court has maintained by the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division. Thus, this decree cannot be nullified under section 6 of the Land Reforms Ordinance. In my view all legal processes as provided in section 6 of the Ordinance does not include a decree of civil Court. Further, the proviso to section 6 of the Ordinance provides that this section shall not apply to acquisition of such homestead under any law. Thus, a decree in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession of homestead land passed by a civil court cannot render nugatory applying section 6 of the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984.
